title: Turn a log line into structure
brief:
A log line looks like `IP - - [ts] "METHOD path" status`. Complete `parse_line` so it returns a tuple `(ip, method, status)` with `status` as an `int`. Empty lines should be skipped.

**Stretch:** make `parse_line` survive a line whose status is not a number — return `None` instead of raising. In a real log pipeline one malformed line must not kill the whole run.
starter:
LOG = '10.0.0.7 - - [15/Oct/2026:09:12:44] "POST /login" 401'

def parse_line(line):
    # return (ip, method, status), or None for empty/malformed lines
    ...
hints: `str.split()` with a maxsplit argument keeps the spaces inside a field — here you need `"METHOD path"` kept together.
Do not reach for a regex first: `parts = line.split()` gives you `['10.0.0.7','-','-','[ts]','"POST','/login"','401']`. Stitch `"METHOD path"` back from two elements.
The output must be a tuple, not a list — tests compare with `==` against `(ip, method, status)`.
tests:
check('ip', parse_line(LOG)[0] == '10.0.0.7', parse_line(LOG))
check('method', parse_line(LOG)[1] == 'POST', parse_line(LOG))
check('status is an int', isinstance(parse_line(LOG)[2], int), type(parse_line(LOG)[2]))
check('empty line', parse_line('') is None)
check('whitespace only', parse_line('   ') is None)
check('too short', parse_line('10.0.0.7 - -') is None)
check('other method', parse_line('1.2.3.4 - - [x] "PATCH /api" 204') == ('1.2.3.4', 'PATCH', 204), parse_line('1.2.3.4 - - [x] "PATCH /api" 204'))

title: Verify a checksum
brief:
You have the file bytes and an expected digest. Complete `sha256_hex` so it returns the hex digest. **Watch the trap**: unbounded `int(digest, 16)` comparisons break on Python 3.11+ (`ValueError` from `int.from_bytes` overflow) — compare strings, always.

**Stretch:** write `verify(data, expected)` that returns `True`/`False` by comparing hex strings with `hmac.compare_digest`. That is the only comparison a checksum in a release pipeline should use.
starter:
import hashlib

DATA = b'anvil-lab'
EXPECTED = '621824640ff85d4bfab5a9092831b8674de5d14b0f1e9c5532e3fb8410f469f0'

def sha256_hex(data: bytes) -> str:
    ...
hints: `hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()` — whether you pass `usedforsecurity` does not matter here, and `hashlib.sha256(data).digest().hex()` works too.
A digest is 32 bytes → 64 hex characters. If you get fewer, you are encoding a `repr` instead of the raw bytes.
`hashlib.sha256(data).digest()` gives raw bytes — `.hex()` on those is the same 64 characters, and it never raises.
solution:
def sha256_hex(data: bytes) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
tests:
check('type', isinstance(sha256_hex(DATA), str))
check('hex digest length', len(sha256_hex(DATA)) == 64)
check('lowercase hex', all(c in '0123456789abcdef' for c in sha256_hex(b'x')))
check('known vector', sha256_hex(b'') == 'e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855')
check('matches expected', sha256_hex(DATA) == EXPECTED, sha256_hex(DATA))
check('different input, different digest', sha256_hex(b'a') != sha256_hex(b'b'))

title: Three layers of encryption
brief:
The payload is base64, under it ROT13, under that a reversed string. Complete `decode_blob` so it returns the plaintext. Two gotchas: `base64.b64decode` needs bytes, and in Python 3 a `str` is not bytes — and `b64decode` does not discard junk by default, so pass `validate=True`.

**Stretch:** handle the case where the payload is *not* base64 at all and return `None` instead of letting the exception escape. Decoders that raise on hostile input are how log parsers get killed.
hints: ROT13 is a 13-character shift in ASCII letters; `str.maketrans` + `str.translate` does it in one line.
Order matters: base64 → ROT13 → reverse the characters. The order is part of the exercise.
`validate=True` turns junk into a `binascii.Error` — decide deliberately whether `decode_blob` should raise or return `None`.
tests:
check('layer 1', rot13('flag{') == 'synt{', rot13('flag{'))
check('rot13 leaves digits alone', rot13('Anvil 123!') == 'Naivy 123!', rot13('Anvil 123!'))
check('empty string', rot13('') == '')
check('final result', decode_blob(BLOB) == 'v3ctor{w4sm_eff3ct}', decode_blob(BLOB))
check('empty payload', decode_blob('') == '', decode_blob(''))

title: Spot an injection attempt
brief:
You get part of an HTTP query. Complete `is_injection` so it returns `True` when the value looks like a SQL injection attempt: `' OR`, `" OR`, `UNION SELECT`, `; DROP`, a `--` comment, or `SLEEP(`. **Do not** treat a literal `%27` (an encoded apostrophe) as an attack — that is a correctly encoded value.

**Stretch:** this lab's filter is a toy. Real WAFs normalise first (unicode, `/*! */`, double encoding). Write `normalise(value)` that collapses whitespace and lowercases, and call it before matching — then explain which attacks still slip through.
hints: Make a list of patterns and use `any()` instead of a pyramid of `if`s.
Normalise the input: `.lower()` plus an extra `' '`, so `'OR` without a space is caught too.
A word-boundary or length check on top of the pattern list keeps false positives down: `1.2.3.4` has digits and dots, but no keyword.
tests:
check('classic OR', is_injection("admin' OR '1'='1") is True)
check('union', is_injection('1 UNION SELECT password FROM users') is True)
check('stacked query', is_injection('admin"; DROP TABLE users;--') is True)
check('time based blind', is_injection("1' AND SLEEP(5)") is True)
check('ordinary text', is_injection('Marian Nowak') is False)
check('an email is not an attack', is_injection('user@example.com') is False)
check('an ip is not an attack', is_injection('10.0.0.1') is False)
check('an encoded apostrophe is not an attack', is_injection('O\'Brien') is False)

title: Enumerable where a loop would go
brief:
This track needs a real interpreter, so in v1 the Ruby labs run in the downloadable lab machine.

```ruby
EVENTS = [{'id' => 4, 'severity' => 'low', 'type' => 'file_open'},
         {'id' => 9, 'severity' => 'high', 'type' => 'exec'},
         {'id' => 2, 'severity' => 'high', 'type' => 'file_open'},
         {'id' => 7, 'severity' => 'low', 'type' => 'auth'},
         {'id' => 1, 'severity' => 'low', 'type' => 'exec'}]

def suspicious(events)
  # return sorted ids where severity == 'high' OR type == 'exec'
end

puts suspicious(EVENTS).inspect  # should print [1, 2, 9]
```

On the lab VM: `bash lab-vm/build.sh --run`, then `labcheck --task rb-01-enumerable`.

**Stretch:** `suspicious` takes a list and returns ids. Add `counts_by(events, key)` — grouping events by severity — and then a one-liner that finds the single most common event type. `each_with_object(Hash.new(0))` is the idiomatic shape.
hints: `events.select { |e| ... }.map { |e| e['id'] }.sort` — the whole pipeline in three steps.
`select` returns elements, not indices — that is why the `map` comes after it.
The checker also runs an empty log and a quiet log: a pipeline that explodes on `[]` is not done.

title: Redact a card number in a log
brief:
Masking card numbers is real work in logs and incident reports, so this lab starts in the downloadable lab machine.

```ruby
def redact(text)
  # return [new_text, replacements_made]
end

p redact('card 4111 1111 1111 1111 declined')  # ['card ****-****-****-1111 declined', 1]
p redact('4111-1111-1111-1111')                # ['****-****-****-1111', 1]
p redact('no data here')                      # ['no data here', 0]
```

On the lab VM: `labcheck --task rb-02-redact`.

**Stretch:** the checker feeds two cards in one line. A counter that only ever returns 0 or 1 passes a careless review — count every replacement, not every line.
hints: `gsub` with a block gives you the match in `$~[0]`, so you can count replacements as you go.
Do not use `gsub` with two string arguments — you only get a replacement counter from the block form.
`$~[0]` inside the block is the whole match, so `m[-4, 4]` keeps the last four digits and the rest becomes asterisks.

title: Predict the output: ownership
choices: `let t = s;` moves the value, so `s` no longer exists and `println!("{}", s)` does not compile
`String` implements `Copy`, so both bindings work and it prints "anvil"
It compiles, but it prints "anvil" twice
It compiles only with an explicit `.clone()` inside `println!`
It compiles only on an older edition, because `String` gained `Copy` at some point
It compiles and the output depends on the optimisation level
explain:
`String` does not implement `Copy` — `let t = s;` is a **move**: the buffer is transferred and the original binding is invalidated. That is why you use `&str` (borrowing, cheap) or `s.clone()`. On the lab VM you run the same program through `cargo build` and read the real error message.

Choice 5 exists to make the point that there is no edition where this changes: `Copy` for heap-backed types is never automatic.

title: Read a borrow checker error
brief:
On the lab VM you hit this error:

```
error[E0382]: borrow of `v` as immutable because it is also borrowed as mutable
  --> src/main.rs:12:18
   |
12 |     v.push(v.len());
   |     ^          ^ borrow of `v` as immutable here
   |     |          first mutable borrow later used by call
```

What is the cleanest fix?
choices: `let n = v.len(); v.push(n);` — end the borrow first, then mutate
`v.push(v.len());` with `#[allow(borrow_check)]` on the function
Change `v` to `Vec<&str>` so `.len()` does not borrow
`let n = &v.len();` so the borrow lasts longer
`let n = v.len(); let first = &v[0]; v.push(n);` — re-borrow after measuring
Split the statement with a semicolon inside the same expression: `v.push({ let n = v.len(); n })`
explain:
The classic "mutable borrow while an immutable borrow is live" problem. Splitting the calls gives both borrows separate, non-overlapping lifetimes. `#[allow(...)]` only silences the diagnostic — the bug comes back as soon as the code changes.

Note that `#[allow(...)]` never fixes a real borrow conflict — it only hides it until someone edits the line.

title: Name the technique in the log
brief:
A fragment of a WAF log from your own environment:

```
10.4.0.19 GET /search?q=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20password%20FROM%20users--&status=200
10.4.0.19 GET /search?q=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20password%20FROM%20users--&status=500
10.4.0.19 GET /admin.php&status=404
```

What is the attack you see in that query?
choices: SQL injection via UNION SELECT (`UNION` combined with a `--` comment to cut off the rest of the query)
Cross-site scripting — the attacker injects `<script>`
Command injection via `|` in the parameter
Directory brute force
Path traversal — the attacker walks up with `../`
HTTP parameter pollution — the same parameter appears twice
explain:
Three features at once: the quote breaks the string literal, `UNION SELECT` appends a second query, and `--` comments out the rest of the original. Where does a successful injection end up? Find out yourself: send the request to the target on the lab VM and see what the database returns.

The distractors matter: each of those is a real attack class you will meet in the VM labs, and none of them matches a quote plus `UNION SELECT` plus `--`.

title: Run a service with an unsafe flag (lab VM)
brief:
This lab series needs a real Linux, a network and a process — none of which can be simulated inside a browser tab. Download the lab VM image (link on the home page), install it and run:

1. `bash lab-vm/build.sh --run`
2. inside the machine: `systemctl start anvil-lab && labcheck --task vm-01`

On purpose you set a flag that leaks data into the log, then confirm the leak with a single command.

title: Write your own scanner with ShadowScan
brief:
A scanner is only useful if you can trust its output. On the lab machine you get a scope file, a request budget and a fixture of canned responses. Write `/home/student/scan.json`: one entry per in-scope host, exactly once each, sorted by host, and never more requests than the budget allows.

```
cat /home/student/targets.txt     # lab-a.internal, lab-b.internal, lab-c.internal
cat /home/student/budget          # 50
cat /home/student/fixtures/responses.json
labcheck --task sec-l1-webscan
```

`lab-d.internal` sits in the fixture on purpose. Including it fails the task: a scanner that walks outside its scope is how real scanners end up in someone else's network.

title: Count requests per client in a sliding window
brief:
Rate limiting only works if the window really slides. You get request timestamps in seconds. Complete `over_limit` so it returns the client ids that sent **more than `limit` requests inside any window of `window` seconds**, sorted by id.

A fixed bucket per minute is the classic bug: an attacker splits the burst across the boundary and gets twice the budget. The window here starts at every single request, not on a boundary.

**Stretch:** a real limiter also has to decide what to do with the request that broke the limit — drop it, or serve a `429`. Return the response too, and show where the budget is spent.
starter:
REQUESTS = [('a', 0), ('a', 1), ('a', 2), ('b', 10), ('a', 2), ('b', 11), ('b', 11)]
SPARSE = [('c', 4), ('c', 6)]

def over_limit(requests, window=3, limit=2):
    # return sorted client ids that exceed the limit inside any sliding window
    ...
hints: Group by client first and sort each list of timestamps — a sliding window needs them ordered.
Two pointers: `hi` walks forward while `times[hi] < t0 + window`, `lo` forward while `times[lo] < t0`. The count is `hi - lo`.
The edge that matters: two requests 2 seconds apart (SPARSE below) sit in different 5-second buckets but in the same sliding window. That is the bug this lab is about.
tests:
check('okno 3s, limit 2: obaj klienci', over_limit(REQUESTS, window=3, limit=2) == ['a', 'b'], over_limit(REQUESTS, window=3, limit=2))
check('okno 3s, limit 4: nikt', over_limit(REQUESTS, window=3, limit=4) == [], over_limit(REQUESTS, window=3, limit=4))
check('okno przesuwne, nie kubełek', over_limit(SPARSE, window=5, limit=1) == ['c'], over_limit(SPARSE, window=5, limit=1))
check('pustka to nie atak', over_limit([]) == [])

title: Safe FFI to eBPF
brief:
`bpf_probe_read_user` returns a negative errno and leaves the destination buffer untouched when it fails. Wrap it so a caller can never receive a half-filled buffer, and never panic on a short read.

```
cd /home/student/ffi
cargo test                       # your own #[cfg(test)] module
labcheck --task rs-l1-ffi        # builds and runs the tests for you
```

This is the same shape as the wrapper in talus-process-monitor: the kernel call is unsafe, so the safe surface has to do the checking.

title: Decode a JWT and spot the unsigned one
brief:
A JWT is three base64**url** parts separated by dots. Complete `decode_payload` so it returns the payload as a dictionary, and `is_unsigned` so it reports a token whose header says `alg: none`. Two traps: base64url uses `-`/`_` instead of `+`/`/` and drops the `=` padding, and `json.loads` raises on garbage — a malformed token must give `None`, not an exception.

**Stretch:** add `header(token)` and read the `alg` value. Then: which other algorithms would you refuse outright, and where does that decision belong — in the library or in your code?
starter:
import base64, json

TOKEN = 'eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjMiLCJyb2xlIjoiYWRtaW4ifQ.c2lnbmF0dXJl'
NONE_TOKEN = 'eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJzdWIiOiIxIn0.'

def decode_payload(token: str):
    # return the payload dict, or None for anything malformed
    ...

def is_unsigned(token: str) -> bool:
    ...
hints: `base64.urlsafe_b64decode(part + '=' * (-len(part) % 4))` — the padding has to come back.
`is_unsigned` decodes the *header*, not the payload: `json.loads` the first part and look at `alg`.
Never trust the claims before verifying the signature — `decode_payload` here parses an *unverified* payload. That is exactly what an `alg: none` token exploits.
tests:
check('payload', decode_payload(TOKEN) == {'sub': '123', 'role': 'admin'}, decode_payload(TOKEN))
check('sub claim', decode_payload(TOKEN)['sub'] == '123')
check('garbage is None', decode_payload('nope') is None)
check('too few parts', decode_payload('a.b') is None)
check('dots only', decode_payload('...') is None)
check('alg none detected', is_unsigned(NONE_TOKEN) is True)
check('signed token is not unsigned', is_unsigned(TOKEN) is False)
check('empty token', is_unsigned('') is False)

title: Count who is hammering the service
brief: A firewall log, one line per request. Complete `top_ips` so it returns the addresses seen **at least `threshold` times** (the default is 2 — anything seen once is noise), busiest first, each as an `(ip, count)` tuple. Lines that do not start with an IP address should be skipped, not crash the run — log files are full of continuation lines.
starter:
LOG = '''10.0.0.7 GET /login 401
10.0.0.7 GET /admin 403
10.0.0.9 GET / 200
broken line without an address
10.0.0.7 GET /wp-admin 404
192.168.1.4 GET / 200
192.168.1.4 POST /login 401'''

def top_ips(lines, threshold=2):
    # return [(ip, count), ...] for addresses above the threshold, busiest first
    ...
hints: A quick filter is `line.split()[0].count('.') == 3` — IPv4 has three dots, and a broken line has no token at all.
`collections.Counter` then a sorted comprehension over `items()` with `reverse=True` does the rest.
`threshold` is inclusive: `count >= threshold`, not `>`. A `>` there silently drops every address seen exactly `threshold` times.
tests:
check('busiest first', top_ips(LOG.splitlines())[0] == ('10.0.0.7', 3), top_ips(LOG.splitlines()))
check('full ranking', top_ips(LOG.splitlines()) == [('10.0.0.7', 3), ('192.168.1.4', 2)], top_ips(LOG.splitlines()))
check('a single hit is noise', ('10.0.0.9', 1) not in top_ips(LOG.splitlines()))
check('threshold=3 hides the pair', top_ips(LOG.splitlines(), threshold=3) == [('10.0.0.7', 3)], top_ips(LOG.splitlines(), threshold=3))
check('threshold=1 counts singletons', top_ips(['10.0.0.1 GET / 200'], threshold=1) == [('10.0.0.1', 1)])
check('a broken line does not crash', top_ips(['broken', '', '10.0.0.1 GET / 200']) == [])
setup:
LOG = '''10.0.0.7 GET /login 401
10.0.0.7 GET /admin 403
10.0.0.9 GET / 200
broken line without an address
10.0.0.7 GET /wp-admin 404
192.168.1.4 GET / 200
192.168.1.4 POST /login 401'''

title: Predict the output: a reference outlives its owner
choices: It does not compile: `&owned` would return a reference to a local that is dropped at the end of the function (E0515)
It compiles and returns a slice of the owned copy, which lives on the heap
It compiles only with an explicit lifetime annotation like `fn longest<'a>(word: &'a str) -> &'a str`
It compiles and the value is copied to the caller's stack frame
It compiles because the heap allocation outlives the binding
It compiles if you annotate the return type as `&'static str`
explain:
This is E0515, *cannot return reference to local variable*. The heap allocation survives, but the **binding** `owned` dies with the function, so the borrow checker refuses — it tracks what may be dropped, not where bytes live. Return `String` and let the caller own it, or hand back the input reference with a matching lifetime. Run it on the lab VM and read the message yourself.

The compiler is tracking *values that may be dropped*, not memory addresses. That is why `Box::leak` exists.
